name: Job
sourceNote: Written freshly, thought for thought, from the oldest Hebrew, Greek, and Aramaic witnesses (the Masoretic Text with the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Septuagint, and the Samaritan Pentateuch). © 2026 Jose Santiago. All rights reserved.

verses.text: In the land of Uz{b} lived Job.{a} Nothing in his life was crooked. He respected God and wanted nothing to do with evil.
He had seven sons and three daughters.
Job’s wealth was 3,000 camels, 7,000 sheep, 500 female donkeys, and 500 teams of oxen,{c} plus a great crowd of servants. In all the east, no one had more than Job.{d}
Job’s sons took turns holding a feast, each in his own home on his own day. They always invited their three sisters to come and eat and drink with them.

When a round of feasts was over, Job would call his children to him and set them apart for God. Early the next morning he would give a burnt offering for each child. He thought, “Maybe my children sinned and turned against God{e} in their hearts.” Job did this every time.
One day the heavenly beings{f} came to stand before Yahweh. The Adversary{g} came with them.
Yahweh asked the Adversary, “Where have you been?” The Adversary answered, “I have been wandering all over the earth, going back and forth.”
Then Yahweh said, “Did you notice my servant Job? There is nobody like him in the world. His life is straight and good. He respects God and avoids evil.”
The Adversary replied, “Does Job honor God for nothing?
You have put a fence around him, around his family, and around everything he owns. You have made all his work succeed, and his animals cover the land.
But reach out and take away all that he has. I promise you, he will curse{h} you to your face.”
Yahweh said to the Adversary, “All right. Everything he owns is in your hands. Only do not touch Job himself.” So the Adversary left Yahweh’s presence.
One day Job’s sons and daughters were feasting at the home of the oldest brother.
A messenger ran to Job and said, “Your oxen were plowing, and the donkeys were eating close by.
Sabean{i} raiders swooped in and took every animal. They struck the servants down with swords. Only I escaped, and I came to tell you.”
He had not finished when a second man arrived. “Fire from God{j} fell out of the sky,” he said. “Sheep and servants burned up together. I alone escaped to bring you word.”

He had not finished when a third man arrived. “Chaldean raiders came in three groups,” he said. “They rushed the camels and seized them. They killed the servants with swords. Only I escaped to bring you word.”
He had not finished when a fourth man arrived. “Your sons and daughters were feasting at their oldest brother’s house.
Out of the desert a strong wind rushed in. It hit the house at all four corners, and the walls came down on the young people. They have died. Only I escaped to bring you word.”
Job got up and ripped his robe apart. He shaved his head. Then he dropped to the ground in worship.

He said,
“I came out of my mother with nothing,
and I will go back with nothing.{k}
Yahweh gave, and Yahweh has taken away.
May Yahweh’s name be praised.”
Even then, Job did not sin. He never blamed God for any wrong.

notes.text: The meaning of the name Job is uncertain. Some suggest “Where is my father?” and others “one who is hated.”
The place called Uz is not certain. It was probably east or southeast of Israel, near Edom.
Original: “five hundred yoke of oxen.” A yoke is a pair of oxen joined for plowing.
Original: “the greatest of all the sons of the east,” that is, the peoples living in the desert east of Israel.
The Hebrew says “blessed God” here and in verse 11. It is a polite way of saying “cursed,” which scribes did not want to write.
Original: “sons of God” (Hebrew bene ha-elohim), the heavenly beings who serve God. The Septuagint says “angels of God.”
Original: “the satan” (Hebrew ha-satan), meaning “the accuser” or “the opponent.” In chapters 1 and 2 it is a title, not yet a personal name. The Septuagint says “the devil.”
Original: “bless.” See the note at verse 5.
The Sabeans were probably raiders from Sheba in southern Arabia. The Septuagint says “robbers.”
Probably lightning. Original: “fire of God” (or “a terrible fire”).
“Go back” probably means to the earth, the mother of all, or to the grave.

verses.text: Another day came when the heavenly beings{a} stood before Yahweh. The Adversary came with them to stand before Yahweh.
Yahweh asked the Adversary, “Where have you been?” He answered, “I have been wandering all over the earth, going back and forth.”

Yahweh said, “Did you notice my servant Job? Nobody on earth compares with him. His life is straight and good. He respects God and avoids evil. Even now he holds on to his goodness, though you stirred me up to destroy him without cause.”
“Skin for skin!”{b} the Adversary answered. “People will pay anything to keep their lives.
Now reach out and hurt his body, his flesh and his bones. I promise you, he will curse{c} you right to your face.”
“Go ahead,” Yahweh said to the Adversary. “He is yours to hurt. But you must not take his life.”
The Adversary left Yahweh’s presence and struck Job with painful sores,{d} covering him from his feet to the top of his head.
Sitting in the ashes,{e} Job scraped his skin with a broken piece of pottery.
His wife asked, “Will you keep on holding to your goodness? Curse{f} God, and die!”{g}
But Job told her, “That is how a senseless woman talks. We take good from God’s hand. Shall we not take bad too?” In all of this, Job’s lips did not sin.

Three friends of Job heard about all his troubles. They came from different places: Eliphaz from Teman, then Bildad from Shuah, then Zophar from Naamah.{h} They set a time to meet, and they went to give him sympathy and comfort.
They saw him from far off and could not tell who he was. They began to sob loudly. Each one ripped his robe and tossed dust into the air so it fell on his head.
Seven days and seven nights they sat on the ground beside Job. No one spoke to him, because they could see how deep his pain was.

notes.text: Original: “sons of God.” See the note at 1:6.
This saying is probably from trading: you give up one skin to keep another. Its exact meaning is uncertain.
Original: “bless.” See the note at 1:5.
The Hebrew does not say what the illness was. It may have been boils or another skin disease.
The Septuagint says he sat on a heap of trash outside the city.
Original: “bless.” See the note at 1:5.
The Septuagint has a much longer speech here. In it Job’s wife grieves for their lost children and her own hard wandering, and she ends by telling him to speak against the Lord and die.

Eliphaz may mean “God is pure gold” (uncertain). Teman was a region of Edom. Bildad is uncertain; it may mean “Bel has loved.” Shuah was a son of Abraham (Genesis 25:2). Zophar may mean “sparrow” (uncertain). The place Naamah is not known. The Septuagint calls the three men kings of Teman, Shuah, and the Minaeans.

verses.text: Finally Job broke the silence. He put a curse on the day of his birth.
These were his words:

“Let the day I was born disappear,
and the night that cried, ‘A boy has been conceived!’

Make that day black as night.
May God above forget it.
May no light shine on it.

Let gloom and deep darkness{a} take it back.
Let a cloud sit over it.
Let whatever darkens a day{b} fill it with fear.

Let darkness seize that night.
Do not let it be added to the days of the year,
or counted in any month.

Let that night be empty and silent.
May no cheer be heard in it.

Let people who put curses on days curse it,
those who are skilled at waking Leviathan.{c}

May its evening stars stay dark.
May it hope for dawn and get none.
May it never see the first blink of morning.

That night never closed my mother’s womb.
It never kept trouble away from my eyes.

“Why didn’t I die at birth?
Why didn’t I take one breath and die as I came out?

Why were there knees to hold me
and breasts to feed me?

If I had died, I would be lying quiet now.
I would be asleep and at peace,

They sat with kings and advisers of the earth,
who had ruins rebuilt for their own fame,{d}

or with rulers who owned gold
and filled their houses with silver.

Or why was I not buried like a baby born dead,
like infants who never saw the light?

In the grave the wicked stop their trouble-making,
and worn-out people rest.

Prisoners relax together there.
They no longer hear a guard shouting.

Great and small are all the same there,
and the slave is free from his owner.

“Why does God give light to those in pain,
and life to those with bitter hearts?

They long for death, but it will not come.
They hunt for it harder than for hidden treasure.

They would be thrilled
and would cheer if they found the grave.

Why give life to a man whose way is lost,
a man God has walled in?

Sighing is what I eat instead of bread.
My groans spill out like water from a jar.

What I was most afraid of has happened to me.
What I dreaded has found me.

I have no peace and no quiet.
I cannot rest, because trouble keeps coming.”

notes.text: The Hebrew word is tsalmawet, often translated “shadow of death.” Many scholars read it as “deep darkness.” The same word is used in other places in Job.
The Hebrew phrase is rare and uncertain. It may mean eclipses or “things that darken the day.”
Leviathan was a sea monster in ancient stories, a picture of chaos (see 41:1; Psalm 74:14). Some scholars read “those who curse the sea” instead.
Or “built tombs for themselves,” perhaps pyramids. The Hebrew is uncertain. The Septuagint says “who were proud of their swords.”

subheads.20: Why Give Life to the Miserable?

verses.text: Then Eliphaz from Teman answered:

“May I say something to you? Will it tire you out?
I cannot keep quiet any longer.

You have taught many people.
You have strengthened weak hands.

Your words picked up those who stumbled.
You steadied knees that were giving way.

Now trouble has come to you, and you fall apart.
It has touched you, and you are terrified.

Surely your respect for God gave you courage,
and your honest life gave you hope.

Think back. Has an innocent person ever been destroyed?
Where were good people ever wiped out?

I have seen it myself: those who plow evil
and plant trouble harvest the same.

One breath from God destroys them.
A blast of his anger finishes them.

Lions may roar and snarl,
yet the teeth of the young ones are smashed.{a}

The old lion dies with no prey to catch,
and the lioness’s cubs scatter.

“Quietly, a message came my way.
My ear picked up just a murmur.

It came in disturbing thoughts at night,
when deep sleep falls on people.

Terror and shaking seized me.
All my bones trembled.

A spirit{b} passed in front of my face,
and the hair on my skin stood up.

It stopped, but I could not tell what it looked like.
A shape stood before my eyes.
It was quiet, and then I heard a voice:

‘Could any mortal be in the right before God?{c}
Could any person be pure before his Maker?

God does not even trust his own servants.
He finds fault with his angels.

Even weaker are those who live in clay houses,
whose footing is dust,
and who are squashed like a moth!

Between sunrise and sunset they are smashed.
No one pays attention, and they are gone for good.

The rope of their tent is pulled out.
They die without gaining wisdom.’”

notes.text: Verses 10 and 11 use five different Hebrew words for lion. Their exact differences are uncertain.
Or “a wind” or “a breath.”
Hebrew Eloah, a poetic form of the word for God. It appears about forty times in Job. Or “More right than his God? More clean than his Maker?”

verses.text:
“Shout for help if you want. Will anyone reply?
Which of the holy ones{a} could you ask?

Anger kills a foolish man,
and jealousy kills a simple one.

I watched a fool put down roots,
and soon I declared his house under a curse.

His children are far from safe.
They are crushed in court, and no one rescues them.

Trouble does not come up out of the dust,
and misery does not grow from the ground.

Human beings are born to trouble,
just as flames{d} shoot up from a fire.

“As for me, I would go to God
and place my cause in his hands.

He does great things too deep to understand,
and wonders too many to count.

He sends rain on the land.
He pours water over the fields.

He lifts the humble up high.
He raises those who mourn to safety.

He ruins the schemes of the crafty,
so their hands cannot finish what they plan.{e}

He traps the clever in their own cunning.{f}
The plots of crooked people rush to a quick end.

They meet darkness in the day.
At midday they fumble about like those in the night.

He rescues the poor from the sword in the cruel mouth,
and out of the fists of the mighty.

That gives the weak some hope,
and wrong has to close its mouth.

“Happy is the person God corrects!
So do not hate the training of Shaddai.{g}

He hurts, but he also bandages.
He wounds, and his hands heal.

Six times he will pull you out of trouble.
The seventh time, harm still will not touch you.

When hunger comes, he will buy you back from death.
In war, he will keep the sword from you.

You will be hidden from slander,
and not afraid when ruin comes.

You will laugh at ruin and hunger.
You will not fear the wild animals.

You will have an agreement with the field stones,
and the wild beasts will live in peace with you.

You will know your tent is safe.
You will check your flock and find none missing.

You will see your children grow into many,
your descendants as many as blades of grass.

You will reach the grave in old age,{h}
like a bundle of grain gathered in its season.

We have looked into all this, and it holds true.
Listen, and learn it for yourself.”

notes.text: That is, heavenly beings.
The Hebrew of this line is hard to understand.
So several ancient versions. The Hebrew word is uncertain and is often read as “a trap.”
Original: “sons of Resheph.” Resheph was a Canaanite god of plague and fire. The phrase may mean sparks or birds of prey. The Septuagint says “the young of the vulture fly high.”
The Hebrew word for “what they plan” is rare. It may mean “success” or “anything lasting.”
Paul quotes this line in 1 Corinthians 3:19.
Shaddai is an old name for God. It is often translated “the Almighty,” but its meaning is uncertain (see the note at Genesis 17:1). It appears 31 times in Job and is kept as a name.
The Hebrew word is found only here and in 30:2. “Old age” is a guess from the setting.

verses.text: Job answered:

“If only my grief could be put on a scale,
with all my misery set on the other side!

It would outweigh the sand of the seas.
No wonder my words have come out wild.{a}

The arrows of Shaddai are stuck in my body.
My spirit drinks their venom.
God’s terrors are lined up to fight me.

Does a wild donkey cry out while it grazes on green grass?
Does a bull bawl over a full trough?

Who eats bland food with no salt?
Who enjoys the slimy juice of a plant?{b}

I refuse to touch such things.
They make me sick like spoiled food.{c}

“How I long for my request to be granted!
How I long for God to give me what I hope for!

Let God decide to crush me.
Let him pull back his hand and finish me off.

Then I would still find one comfort,
and I would leap{d} with joy in spite of merciless pain:
I never hid the words of the Holy One.

What strength do I have, that I should keep waiting?
What future do I have, that I should be patient?

Am I made of stone?
Is my skin made of bronze?

I have no help left inside me.
Any success{e} has been chased from me.

“A friend should show loyalty to someone about to collapse,
even if he has lost his respect for Shaddai.{f}

But my brothers have proved false, like a seasonal stream,
like streambeds that run dry.

Dark ice covers them in winter,
and melting snow flows into them.

In the hot season they stop flowing and vanish.
When the heat comes, they disappear from their beds.

Travelers turn off their path to find water.
They walk into the empty desert and die.

Caravans from Tema looked for water there.
Traveling groups from Sheba counted on it.

They were let down by their hope.
They arrived and were bitterly disappointed.

You have turned out the same.{g}
A terrible sight appears, and you run in fear.

Have I begged you for a present?
Have I asked you to pay out your savings for me?

Did I say, ‘Rescue me from my enemy’?
Or, ‘Pay a price to free me from cruel men’?

“Teach me, and I will keep quiet.
Show me where I went wrong.

Honest words can be so strong!
But what does your arguing prove?

Do you plan to correct my words?
A desperate man’s speech is only wind.

You would even gamble over an orphan,
and sell out your own friend.

Now please, look at me.
I would never lie to your faces.

Think again. Do not be unfair.
Think again, for I am still in the right.

Is there any lie on my tongue?
Can I not taste the bitterness of disaster?”

notes.text: The Hebrew word is rare. It may mean “wild” or “stammering.”
The Hebrew word is found only here. It may mean the juice of a plant, or the white of an egg. This is uncertain.
The Hebrew of this line is uncertain.
The Hebrew word is found only here. “Jump” is a guess; it may mean “shrink back.”
The Hebrew word for “success” is the same as in 5:12.
The Hebrew of this verse is uncertain.
The Hebrew is hard. Some copies say “you have become nothing.” The Septuagint says “You too have come to me without pity.”

subheads.1: Job Replies: My Pain Is Heavy
subheads.14: Friends Who Fail Like a Dry Stream

verses.text:
“Does anyone on earth have more than hard work to do?
Are our days not like those of a paid worker?

Like a slave who longs for evening shade,
like a worker who waits for his wages,

I have been given empty months,
and nights of misery were handed to me.

Worms and scabs cover my body.
My skin cracks open and oozes.

My days race by, quicker than a weaver’s shuttle,
and they run out with nothing to hope for.{b}

“Think of it, God: my life is a puff of air.
Good days will not come to my eyes again.

Whoever sees me now will not see me later.
You will look for me, and I will be gone.

Clouds fade and drift off.
So anyone who goes down to the grave{c} will never climb out.

He never goes back to his house.
The people of his town will forget him.

“That is why I will not keep my lips sealed.
My spirit is in anguish, and I will say so.
My soul is bitter, and I will complain.

Am I the Sea? Am I the Dragon?{d}
Why else would you put a guard on me?

I tell myself, ‘My bed will bring comfort.
Lying down will lighten my complaints.’

But then you frighten me with dreams,
and scare me with visions.

I would rather be choked,
rather die than live in this body.

I despise my life. I will not live on and on.
Leave me be, for my days are empty.

“What are people, that you pay them so much attention,
that you set your mind on them,

check on them every morning,
and test them every minute?

Will you never glance away?
Can you not leave me alone for even a moment?

If I did sin, how did that hurt you,
you who watch over people?
Why make me your target?
Why have I become a load to myself?{e}

Why will you not pardon my wrongdoing
and sweep away my guilt?
Soon I will be lying in the dirt.
When you come looking, I will not be there.”

notes.text: The Hebrew word is uncertain. It may mean “the evening stretches out.”
The Hebrew word for “hope” can also mean “thread.” This is a play on words with the weaver’s shuttle.
Original: Sheol, the Hebrew name for the place of the dead.
The Sea and the Dragon were wild sea monsters in ancient stories. Compare 3:8.
The Hebrew text says “a load to myself.” An old scribal tradition and the Septuagint say “a load to you.”

subheads.7: My Life Is Only a Breath
subheads.17: What Are People to You, God?

verses.text: Then Bildad from Shuah answered:

“How long will you keep talking this way?
Your words are a huffing, puffing wind.

Does God twist what is fair?
Does Shaddai bend what is right?

Maybe your children sinned against him.
Then he handed them over to the result of their sin.

But if you search for God with all your heart
and plead with Shaddai for mercy,

and if you are clean and honest,
then he will rise up for you
and give you back your true home.

Your first days were small,
but your last days will be very great.

“Go ahead and ask the earlier generation.
Think about what their parents found out.

We arrived only yesterday and know little.
Our time on earth is as short as a passing shadow.

Will they not teach you and tell you?
Will they not speak from what they understand?

Does papyrus{a} shoot up where no marsh exists?
Do reeds grow tall with no water around them?

Even while they are green and uncut,
they dry up faster than any other plant.

So it is with all who forget God.
The hope of the godless dies out.

What they lean on snaps,{b}
and what they trust is a spider’s house.{c}

They lean on their house, but it will not hold.
They grab it, but it will not last.

Picture a well-watered plant in the sun,
with shoots spreading over its garden.

Its roots coil around a heap of stones.
It searches for a home among the rocks.{d}

But if someone rips it from its place,
that place will say, ‘I have never seen you.’

That is the happy end of that road.{e}
New plants will sprout from the same soil.

“Look, God does not turn away an honest person.
He does not take the hand of those who do evil.

He will still fill your mouth with laughter,
and your lips with cheers.

Your haters will be dressed in shame,
and the tent of the wicked will be gone.”

notes.text: The papyrus is a tall water plant that grows in the marshes along the Nile.
The Hebrew word is found only here. It may mean “snaps” or “is a thin thread.”
That is, a spider’s web.
Or “it lives among stones.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
Bildad says this with irony: the plant’s “joy” is that it is replaced.

subheads.20: God Will Not Reject the Honest

verses.text: Then Job replied:

“Yes, I know this is true.
But how could a mortal ever be found right before God?

Suppose someone wished to argue with him.
Out of a thousand charges, he could not answer even one.

God is wise and powerful.
Who has stood against him and stayed unhurt?

He moves mountains, and they never know it.
In his anger he flips them over.

He jolts the earth out of its place,
and its supports rattle.

He speaks to the sun, and it stays down.
He locks the stars away.

He alone unrolls the sky
and strides across the sea’s high waves.{a}

He set the Bear in the sky, and Orion,
the Pleiades,{b} and the star groups of the south.

He does great things too deep to understand,
and wonders too many to count.

He goes past me, yet I do not see him.
He moves on, yet I never notice.

If he snatches something, who can make him return it?
Who dares to ask him, ‘What is it you are doing?’

“God never calls back his anger.
Rahab’s{c} helpers crouched down beneath him.

So how could I give him an answer?
How could I choose the words to debate him?

Though in the right, I would have no reply.
I could only beg my judge for mercy.

If I called him and he replied,
I still would not believe he had listened.

He batters me with a storm
and adds to my wounds for no reason.

He will not allow me a breath of rest.
He feeds me one bitter thing after another.

If strength is the question, he is the mighty one!
If fairness is the question, who can summon him to court?{d}

Even if I were right, my mouth would find me guilty.
Even if I were blameless, it would show me to be crooked.

I am blameless, yet I do not care what happens.
I despise my life.

It makes no difference, so I say,
‘He ends the lives of the innocent and the wicked alike.’

When a sudden plague kills,
he laughs at the fear of the blameless.

The earth is handed over to wicked people.
He covers the eyes of its judges.
If he is not the one, who is?

“My days run faster than a runner.
They fly away and see nothing good.

They glide past like boats made of reeds,{e}
like an eagle diving at its food.

Suppose I say, ‘I will forget my complaint.
I will drop this sad face and smile.’

I still shake at all my pain,
because I know you will not call me innocent.

I will be found guilty anyway,
so why wear myself out for nothing?

If I scrubbed myself with snow
and washed my hands with soap,{f}

Then you would toss me into a filthy ditch,
and even my clothes would be disgusted by me.

God is no human being like me, so I have no way to answer.
The two of us cannot walk into court together.

No umpire{g} stands between us,
no one to lay a hand on us both.

He should take his stick away from me.
His terror should no longer scare me.

Then I could talk with no fear of him.
But as things stand, I cannot.”

notes.text: Original: “backs.” It may mean the waves or the back of the sea monster. Compare 3:8.

The Hebrew names (Ash, Kesil, Kimah) are uncertain; they are the Bear, Orion, and the Pleiades star groups. Compare 38:31–32 and Amos 5:8. The Septuagint names the Pleiades, the evening star, and Arcturus.

Rahab was a sea monster in ancient stories, a picture of chaos. She is not Rahab of Jericho; the names are spelled differently in Hebrew. Compare 26:12. The Septuagint says “the great sea monsters under heaven.”
The Hebrew may be quoting God’s answer. Many read “who can call him to court?” The line is uncertain.
Light boats made from papyrus reeds (Isaiah 18:2).
Original: “lye,” a cleaner made from plant ashes.
Or “mediator.” The Hebrew word means someone who can judge between two sides. Some old copies read “If only we had an umpire between us.”

subheads.1: How Can a Person Argue with God?
subheads.13: God Is Too Strong to Face

verses.text:
“I am sick of living.
I will let my complaint pour out.
I will talk, even though my soul is bitter.

I will tell God, ‘Do not declare me guilty.
Show me what charge you have against me.

Does it please you to be cruel,
to throw away what your own hands made,
while you smile on the plans of wicked people?

Do you have eyes of flesh?
Do you see the way a human sees?

Are your days as short as ours?
Are your years like a person’s years?

Why do you go digging for my fault
and hunting for my sin?

You know very well I am not guilty,
yet nobody can free me from your grip.

“‘Your hands formed me and shaped me,
every part of me. And now you destroy me?

You worked me as a potter works clay.
Do you plan now to crumble me into dust?

You poured me out like milk, did you not?
You made me firm like cheese.

You covered me in skin and flesh.
You laced me up with bones and muscles.

You gave me life and loyal love.
Your watchful care kept my spirit safe.

Yet you hid another plan in your heart.
I know what you had in mind:

If I sinned, you would be watching,
and you would never let my guilt go.

If I am guilty, how terrible for me!
And if I am innocent, I still cannot hold my head up,
for I am full of shame and soaked in suffering.

If I stand tall, you stalk me like a lion.
Once more you display your amazing strength against me.

“‘Why did you ever let me be born?
I should have died, and no one would have looked on me.

I would have been as if I never lived,
carried straight from birth to the grave.

My days are few. Stop!{b}
Turn away from me for a little cheer,

before I leave and do not come back,
for the land of darkness and gloom,

notes.text: Or “waves of soldiers come against me.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
This follows the written Hebrew. The reading handed down by scribes is “Stop, and leave me alone.”
The Hebrew word for this darkness is rare.

subheads.8: You Made Me. Will You Destroy Me?

verses.text: Then Zophar from Naamah answered:

“Should such a flood of words go without a reply?
Should a big talker{a} be called right?

Will your chatter silence everyone?
Will you jeer and no one make you blush?

You claim, ‘What I believe is spotless,
and you can find no fault in me.’

If only God would talk!
If only he would open his lips and answer you,

“Can you search out the deep secrets of God?
Can you map the far edge of Shaddai?

They are higher than the heavens. What can you do?
They are deeper than the grave. What can you know?

Their measure stretches past the earth
and reaches wider than the sea.

If he comes along and locks someone up,
or calls the court together, who can stop him?

He knows who is worthless.
He sees evil, and he takes notice.

A stupid man will become wise
on the day a wild donkey’s colt is born as a human.{d}

“But if you turn your heart to him
and spread out your hands in prayer,

and if you throw away any sin in your hands
and let no wrong live in your tents,

then you can hold your head high with no stain.
You will stand firm and never be afraid.

You will put your misery out of mind.
It will be like floodwater that ran by long ago.

Your life will blaze brighter than noon.
Even the dark hours will glow like dawn.

You will be bold, since hope is real.
Looking about you,{e} you will lie down in peace.

You will lie down with no one to scare you,
and many will ask for your help.

But the wicked will go blind with worry.
They will find no place to hide.
Their only hope is their last breath.”

notes.text: Original: “a man of lips,” that is, a man full of talk.
The Hebrew word for “wisdom” is the same as in 5:12.
Or “God lets some of your guilt be forgotten.”
Or “when a wild donkey is born tame.” This saying is uncertain.
Or “you will dig a place,” that is, set up your tent. The Hebrew is uncertain.

subheads.13: Return to God and Be Safe

verses.text: Then Job replied:

“No doubt you are the only wise people,
and wisdom will die when you do!

But my mind works as well as yours.
I am not below you.
Who has not heard such things?

My friends laugh at me,
a man who prayed to God and was answered.
Yes, they laugh at a good and honest man.

People at ease look down on those in trouble.
They kick those whose feet are slipping.{a}

“Go ahead, question the cattle, and they will teach you.
Question the birds overhead, and they will inform you.

Or speak to the earth,{c} and it will show you.
Let the sea’s fish tell you the story.

Which of them does not know
that Yahweh’s{d} hand has done this?

Every living thing has its life in his hand,
as does the breath of all people.

The ear tests words
the way the tongue tests food.

Wisdom belongs to the old.
Understanding comes with long life.

“God owns wisdom and power.
Counsel and understanding are his too.

What he tears down cannot be rebuilt.
Whoever he locks up cannot get out.

If he holds back the rain, the land dries up.
If he lets it loose, it floods the earth.

Strength and success are his.
The one who is fooled and the one who fools are both his.

He leads advisers away barefoot and ruined.
He turns judges into fools.

He loosens the chains of kings,
then ties a cloth around their waists.

He leads priests away with nothing.
He topples those who seemed secure.

He silences trusted speakers.
He takes good sense from the elders.

He pours shame on nobles.
He takes the belt of the strong.

He drags deep secrets out of the dark
and brings the deepest gloom into the light.

He makes nations great, then wipes them out.
He lets nations spread, then sends them off as prisoners.

He takes the good sense from leaders of the land
and sets them wandering in a pathless desert.

Without any light they grope in the dark.
He makes them reel like drunks.”

notes.text: The Hebrew of this verse is uncertain.
Or “whom God has put in their hands.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
Or “the plants of the earth.”
This is the only place in the poems of Job (3:1–42:6) where the name Yahweh appears outside the introductions to God’s speeches. Some Hebrew copies say “God.” Compare Isaiah 41:20.

verses.text:
“Look, my own eyes have seen all this.
My ears have heard it and understood.

What you know, I know too.
I am not below you.

But I would rather speak to Shaddai.
I long to argue my case before God.

You, however, smear on lies like plaster.
You are all doctors who cure nothing.

I wish you would keep completely silent.
That, at least, would make you look wise.

Now listen to my argument.
Pay attention to what my lips plead.

Will you speak crooked words to defend God?
Will you tell lies for him?

Will you take his side unfairly?
Will you act as lawyers for God?

Will it turn out well when he looks you over?
Can you trick him as you trick people?

He will surely scold you
if you secretly take sides.

Will his greatness not terrify you?
Will dread of him not fall on you?

Your clever sayings are about as useful as ashes.
Your arguments crumble like clay.

“Be quiet and let me talk.
Then let come what may.

Why do I hold my own flesh in my teeth
and carry my life in my hand?{a}

He may kill me. I have no hope.{b}
But I will still defend my conduct to his face.

Maybe this will even save me,
because a godless man would never dare to stand before him.

Hear my words with care.
Let my statement stay in your ears.

See, my case is ready, laid out in order.
I am sure I will be found right.

Who will bring a charge against me?
If someone does, I will hush and die.

“God, give me just two things,
and I will no longer hide from you.

Take your heavy hand off me,
and do not let your terror frighten me.

Then call me, and I will answer.
Or let me talk, and you reply.

How many wrongs and sins are mine?
Make me see what I did wrong.

Why do you keep your face hidden from me
and count me as your enemy?{c}

Will you terrify a leaf in the wind?
Will you chase dry straw?

You write bitter charges against me.
You hand me the sins I committed when young.

You lock my feet in stocks.
You watch every step I take.
You mark a line{d} around my footprints.

So a person{e} wastes away like rotting wood,
like clothes eaten by moths.

notes.text: This means, “Why do I risk my life?”

This follows the written Hebrew text, which says “not.” The reading handed down by scribes is “in him,” which gives the well-known sense, “Though he kill me, I will hope in him.” The line is hard to settle.
The Hebrew word for “enemy” sounds like Job’s name.
Or “you mark a limit.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
Original: “he,” that is, a human being. This verse may belong after 14:2.

subheads.1: Job Wants to Argue with God

verses.text:
“People are born from women.
Their days are few and crowded with trouble.

They bloom like a flower and then wither.
They run off like a shadow and are gone.

Do you truly fix your gaze on someone like that,
and bring me{a} to court before you?

Who can bring something clean out of something unclean?
No one!

His days are numbered.
You decide how many months he gets.
You set limits that he cannot pass.

So look away from him and let him rest,
until he has enjoyed his day like a hired worker.

“Even a tree has hope.
If it is chopped down, it can sprout again,
and its new shoots will keep coming.

Its roots may age under the soil,
and its stump may die in the ground.

Yet the scent of water makes it bud,
and it grows shoots like a new plant.

A man, though, dies and is laid out flat.
He breathes his last, and where is he?

Water drains out of a lake.
A river shrinks and dries up.

In the same way, people lie down and do not get up.
Until the sky is gone, they will not wake
or rise from their sleep.

“I wish you would tuck me away in the grave,
keep me there until your anger passes,
and set a time to remember me!

If a person dies, can he live again?
I would wait through all the days of my hard labor
until my release{b} came.

You would call, and I would reply.
You would long for what your hands had made.

Then you would count my steps,
but you would not lie in wait for my sin.

You would seal up my wrongs in a pouch
and cover over my guilt.

“But a falling mountain crumbles to nothing,
and a rock slides from its place.

Water wears down stones,
and its floods wash away the soil.
In the same way you wipe out human hope.

You overpower them once and for all, and they go.
You twist their faces and send them away.

Their sons may become honored, but they never know.
They may be brought low, but the dead do not see it.

Each feels only the ache in his own body,
and each grieves only for himself.”

notes.text: The Septuagint, the Syriac, and the Latin read “him.”
The Hebrew word means “change,” “renewal,” or “relief,” like a guard being replaced.

subheads.1: A Short Life Full of Trouble
subheads.7: A Tree Has Hope, but a Person?
subheads.13: If Only I Could Wait in the Grave

verses.text: Then Eliphaz from Teman spoke again:

“Would a wise person reply with hot air
and stuff himself with a scorching desert wind?

Would he argue with useless talk,
with speeches that help no one?

You are even wrecking respect for God,
and you leave no room for prayer to him.

Your guilt is what feeds your mouth.
You have picked the speech of sly people.

Your own mouth convicts you, and I do not have to.
Your lips are your own witnesses.

“Were you the first person ever born?
Were you brought into the world before the hills?

Did you sit in on God’s private council?
Do you keep all wisdom for yourself?

What do you know that we do not?
What do you understand that is hidden from us?

Gray-haired men are on our side,
men older than your own father by many years.

Is the comfort God offers too little for you,
or the kind word we spoke to you?

Why does your heart carry you away?
Why do your eyes flash{a}

as you turn your spirit against God
and let such words fly from your mouth?

Who is any human being, to be pure?
Who is born of a woman, to be good?

God does not even trust his holy ones.
The heavens themselves are not clean before him.

How much less a person who is vile and rotten,
who swallows wrong as easily as water!

“Listen to me, and I will explain.
I will report what I have watched,

what wise men have taught,
and what their ancestors never hid.

Those ancestors alone held the land,
and no outsider lived among them.

The wicked man is in pain all his days.
The cruel man has only a few years left.

The sound of terror rings in his ears.
When all seems calm, a destroyer attacks him.

He cannot believe he will escape the dark.
A sword is waiting for him.

He wanders about asking where his next meal is.{b}
He knows his dark day is near.

Distress and fear terrify him.
They beat him down like a king ready to attack.{c}

He shook his fist at God.
He acted like a hero against Shaddai.

He charged at God with his neck stiff,{d}
behind the thick bumps of his shield.

His face grew fat,
and his waist bulged with flesh.

He lived in towns left in ruins,
in houses where no one should live,
houses that were about to become rubble.

He will not stay rich, and his wealth will not last.
His crops{e} will not bend the ground with their weight.

He will never escape the darkness.
Flames will dry up his branches,
and a puff from God’s{f} mouth will carry him off.

Let him not trust in empty things and fool himself,
for emptiness will be his pay.

It will all come true before his time.
His palm branch will never be green.

Like a vine, he will let his unripe grapes fall.
Like an olive tree, he will drop his blossoms.

Godless crowds will bear no fruit,
and flames will eat the tents of bribe-takers.

They are pregnant with trouble and give birth to evil.
Their wombs are busy with lies.”

notes.text: The Hebrew word is found only here. It may mean “wink” or “flash.”
Or, following the Septuagint, “He is set aside as food for vultures.”
The Hebrew word is found only here. “Ready to attack” is uncertain.
Or “stiff-necked.”
The Hebrew word is found only here. “Crops” is uncertain.
Original: “his,” that is, God’s.

subheads.1: Eliphaz Accuses Job of Empty Talk
subheads.7: Who Do You Think You Are?

verses.text: Then Job replied:

“I have heard plenty like this.
You are all miserable comforters.

Will your windy speeches never end?
What makes you keep answering?

I could talk like you,
if you stood where I stand.
I could string speeches together against you
and wag my head over you.

I could encourage you with my words,
and my lips could soften your pain.

“If I talk, the pain stays.
If I keep still, what do I gain?

God has worn me out.
You have wrecked all my family.

You have made me shrivel,{a} and my thin body speaks against me.
My bony frame stands up and accuses me to my face.

In anger God rips me apart and hates me.
He gnashes his teeth at me.
My foe glares at me with burning eyes.

People hang their mouths open at me.
They slap my cheeks to insult me.
They all crowd together against me.

God hands me over to evil people.
He throws me into the grip of the wicked.

All was calm for me, and he broke me apart.
Seizing my neck, he smashed me to bits.
He set me up as his target.

His archers{b} ring me in.
With no pity he cuts into my insides
and empties my gall onto the ground.

He batters my wall again and again.
He charges me like a fighter.

I have stitched sackcloth over my skin,
and I have buried my pride{c} in the dust.

Weeping has turned my face red,
with dark shadows around my eyes,

though my hands have done no violence,
and my prayer is sincere.

“Earth, do not cover up my blood!
Let my cry never stop echoing.

Even now there is a witness for me in heaven.
My defender is up there on high.{d}

My go-betweens{e} are my friends,
while my eyes pour out tears to God.

I wish someone would argue my case with God,
the way a person speaks up for a friend.

A few more years will pass,
and I will set out on the road with no return.”

notes.text: The Hebrew word is rare. It may mean “seized” or “shriveled.”
Or “his arrows.” The Hebrew word is rare.
Original: “my horn,” which stands for strength or dignity.
The Hebrew word for “witness” is Aramaic and appears only here. People disagree about who it is: God himself or a heavenly helper. Compare 9:33 and 19:25.
Or “my mockers.” The Hebrew word can mean either.

subheads.1: Job Calls His Friends Poor Comforters

verses.text:
“My spirit is used up. My days are put out.
The grave is waiting for me.

Mockers surround me.
My eyes cannot look away from their insults.

Please, God, put up a guarantee for me yourself.
Who else will shake hands and pledge it?{a}

You have shut their minds to understanding,
so you will not let them win.

A man who turns in his friends to share the loot,
his own children’s eyes will fail.

God has made me a joke to the nations,
a man people spit in the face.

My eyes are dim with grief.
My whole body is a shadow.

Honest people are stunned by this.
Those without fault rise up against the godless.

Still, the good person holds to his path,
and the one with clean hands grows stronger.

But all of you, try again if you like.
I will not find one wise man among you.

“My days are over. My plans are shattered,
the dreams{b} of my heart.

These men call night day.
They say light is near, though darkness is here.

If I look to the grave as my only house,
if I spread my bed in the dark,

if I tell the pit,{c} ‘You are my father,’
and tell the worm, ‘You are my mother and sister,’

where then is my hope?
Who could ever find it?

Will it go down with me to the gates of the grave?
Will we all sink into the dust together?”

notes.text: That is, who else will promise to pay for me?
The Hebrew word means “possessions.” Here it probably means “dreams” or “wishes.”
Or “decay.” The Aramaic Targum of Job found at Qumran Cave 11 (11QtgJob) begins to survive from about this verse; its remains cover parts of 17:14 through 42:11.

subheads.11: My Hope Goes Down to the Grave

verses.text: Then Bildad from Shuah spoke again:

“When will you stop hunting for words?{a}
Think first, and then we will talk.

Why do you treat us like animals
and think of us as stupid?{b}

You rip yourself apart in your anger.
Must the whole earth be left empty for you?
Must a mountain crag be shifted?

“Yes, the wicked man’s light will be put out,
and his fire will throw off no sparks.

His tent grows dark inside.
The lamp above him is snuffed out.

His proud steps get short.
His own plans trip him up.

His own feet walk him into a net.
He strolls across a trap.

A snare catches his heel.
A trap holds him tight.

A cord lies buried in the dirt for him,
and a trap is set along his path.

Terrors scare him from every side
and chase right behind him.

Hunger eats his strength,
and disaster waits next to him.

Disease eats his skin.
Death’s firstborn{c} eats his limbs.

Torn out of the tent he trusted,
he is marched away to the king of terrors.

Strangers live in his tent now.{d}
Sulfur is sprinkled on his home like fire.

His roots shrivel underground,
and his branches wilt in the air.

No one remembers him on earth.
His name is gone from the streets.

He is shoved out of the light into darkness
and chased out of the world.

He has no child or grandchild among his people,
and no survivor where he once lived.

People in the west are shocked at his fate,
and people in the east are gripped by horror.{e}

That is what happens to the homes of the wicked,
and to the place of one who does not know God.”

notes.text: The Hebrew word is found only here. It may mean “ends” or “traps.”
Or “unclean.” The Hebrew word is uncertain.
Probably a deadly disease, pictured as the oldest son of Death.
Or “Nothing of his lives in his tent.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
Or “Those who come later are shocked at his day, and those before are gripped by horror.”

subheads.5: The Lamp of the Wicked Goes Out

verses.text: Then Job replied:

“How long will you keep hurting my soul
and crushing me with talk?

Ten times you have insulted me.
You feel no shame as you wrong me.{a}

Even if I really have made a mistake,
the mistake stays with me alone.

If you want to lift yourselves above me
and use my shame as proof against me,

then know this: God is the one who wronged me.
He has thrown his net all around me.

“I shout, ‘Violence!’ but no one answers.
I cry for help, but there is no justice.

He has blocked my path so I cannot pass.
He has put darkness on my road.

My honor he peeled away from me,
and he lifted the crown from my head.

He wrecks me from every side until I am finished.
He yanks up my hope like a tree.

He lights the fire of his anger against me,
and he treats me as his foe.

His troops march up together.
They pile up a ramp against me
and camp around my tent.

“God has pushed my brothers far from me.
Those who knew me now look at me as strangers.

My relatives have given up on me.
My close friends have forgotten me.

People who stay in my house, even my maids, think I am a stranger.
To them I have become a foreigner.

I call for my servant, but he gives no reply,
though I plead with him out loud.

My wife cannot stand my breath.
My own brothers{b} find me disgusting.

Even small children make fun of me.
When I stand up, they talk against me.

All my close friends hate me.
Those I loved have turned on me.

Bones press against my skin and meat.
I have slipped away with just my gums.{c}

Pity me, pity me, my friends,
for God’s hand has hit me hard!

Why do you chase me the way God does?
Have you not eaten enough of me?{d}

“If only my words could be written down!
If only they could be engraved on a scroll,

or cut with an iron pen and lead
into rock to last forever!

As for me, I know that my redeemer{e} lives.
At the end{f} he will rise over the earth.{g}

Even when my skin has been torn off,
I will see God from my own body.{h}

If you say, ‘Let us keep hounding him,
since the cause of his trouble lies in him,’{k}

notes.text: The Hebrew word is found only here. It may mean “wrong” or “stun.”
Original: “the sons of my womb,” that is, my own brothers born of the same mother. The Septuagint says “I begged the sons of my concubines.”
Original: “the skin of my teeth.” This saying is uncertain. It may mean “with nothing at all left.”
This means: by speaking evil of me, as in the Aramaic saying “eat pieces of” someone.

Hebrew go’el, the close relative who buys back family land, frees a relative from slavery, or avenges a death (Leviticus 25:25; Numbers 35:19; Ruth 4:1–6). It is translated “champion” or “defender.” People disagree about whether Job means God himself or another helper in heaven (compare 9:33; 16:19). Verses 25–27 are very hard, and almost every line is uncertain.
Or “as the last one.”
Or “over the dust,” that is, over my grave. The Septuagint says, “I know that he who is about to rescue me is eternal, and will raise up my skin on the earth, which endures these sufferings.”
Or “without my body” (after death) or “in my body.” The Hebrew word can mean either “from within” or “without.”
Or “and not as a stranger.”
Original: “kidneys,” thought of as the place of feelings. It means my heart fails with longing.
This follows many Hebrew copies, the Septuagint, and the Latin. Most Hebrew copies say “in me.”
The Hebrew word is uncertain. Some read “that there is a Judge” or “that there is Shaddai.”

subheads.1: How Long Will You Crush Me?

verses.text: Then Zophar from Naamah replied:

“My troubled thoughts force me to speak up,
because I am so stirred inside.

I hear a scolding that shames me,
and my own understanding tells me how to reply.

Surely you know how it has always been,
ever since people were placed on the earth:

The wicked win only for a short time,
and the godless are glad for just a moment.

Though he rises as high as the sky,
and his head brushes the clouds,

He will disappear for good, like his own garbage.
Those who knew him will ask, ‘Where did he go?’

He flies off like a dream, and no one can find him.
He is chased away like a vision in the night.

Eyes that watched him will not watch again.
His own house will never see him.

His children will beg from the poor,{a}
and his own hands will hand back his riches.

His bones were full of youthful strength,
but that strength will lie with him in the dust.

“Evil tastes sweet in his mouth.
He tucks it under his tongue.

He cannot bear to lose it,
so he holds it against the roof of his mouth.

But in his stomach the food turns sour.
It becomes cobra poison inside him.

He swallowed riches, and he will throw them up.
God will force them out of his stomach.

He sucks cobra venom,
and a viper’s{b} fangs kill him.

He will never enjoy the streams,
the rivers flowing with honey and cream.

He must hand over what he worked for, with nothing to eat.
He gets no pleasure from the money he earned.

He crushed the poor and left them.
He took a house he never built.

“His belly was never still,
so he will not keep the things he craved.

Nothing was left that he did not gobble up,
so his good times will not last.

Even in his fullness, he will be squeezed.
Every hand of the miserable will turn on him.

If he flees from an iron sword,
a bronze-tipped bow will run him through.

He pulls it out, and it comes through his back.
The shining point comes out of his liver.
Terrors close in on him.

Total darkness waits for his treasures.
A fire no one lit will burn him up,
and eat what is left in his tent.

Heaven will lay bare his guilt,
and the earth will stand up against him.

A flood will wash away his household’s goods
on the day God’s{e} anger breaks.

That is the share God gives the wicked,
the property God sets aside for him.”

notes.text: Or “The poor will crush his children.”
The Hebrew word names a poisonous snake. The exact kind is uncertain.
Original: “he.”
The Hebrew word is uncertain. It may mean “into his flesh” or “as his food.”
That is, God’s.

subheads.1: Zophar Says the Wicked Will Not Last

verses.text: Then Job replied:

“Listen closely to my words.
Let that be the comfort you give me.

Put up with me while I speak.
When I finish, you may laugh.

Is my complaint against a human being?
Why should I not lose patience?

Stare at me and be stunned.
Clap a hand across your mouth.

Whenever I think of it, I shake with horror,
and my body trembles.

“Why do wicked people keep on living?
They grow old and become powerful.

They watch their children settle near them,
and their grandchildren grow up in view.

Peace and safety fill their houses.
God’s rod never lands on them.

Their bulls breed every time.
Their cows give birth and never lose a calf.

They let their little ones run out like lambs,
and their children skip and dance.

They sing along with tambourine and harp.
They are happy at the sound of the flute.

They spend their days in comfort,
then go down to the grave{a} in a moment.

And yet they say to God, ‘Leave us alone!
Your ways hold no interest for us.

Who is Shaddai, that we should work for him?
Where is the profit in begging for his help?’

Look: their success is in their own grip.
(The way the wicked plan is not my way.)

“How many times is the wicked man’s lamp snuffed out?
How often does ruin fall on them?
How often does God deal out suffering in his fury?

How many are blown like straw before the wind,
or like dry husks that a storm carries off?

You say, ‘God saves up a man’s guilt for his children.’
No, let God pay it back to the man himself, so he will feel it!

Let him see his own downfall with his own eyes.
Let him drink the fury of Shaddai himself.

Once his months run out,
what does he care about the house he leaves behind?

Can anyone teach God anything,
when God judges even those on high?

One man dies strong and full of life,
completely comfortable and safe,

his body well fed{b}
and his bones full of marrow.

Another dies bitter in spirit,
never having tasted anything good.

Together they lie in the dirt,
and maggots cover them both.

“I know what you are thinking,
and the plots you have against me.

You ask, ‘Where is the palace of the ruler?
Where are the tents the wicked once lived in?’

Have you never asked travelers?
Do you not accept what they report,

that the wicked are spared on the day of disaster,
and carried to safety on the day of anger?{c}

Who tells him to his face what he has done?
Who pays him back for his actions?

When he is carried to the cemetery,
guards stand watch at his tomb.

The dirt of the valley feels soft to him.
A crowd follows him to the grave,
and countless others went before him.

So how can you comfort me with nonsense,
when your replies are nothing but lies?”

notes.text: Or “in peace they go down to the grave.”
The Hebrew word is found only here. It may mean “his pails” or “his sides.” The Septuagint says “his insides are full of fat.”
That is, they are rescued. Or “they are led away from the day of anger.”

subheads.1: Job Asks Why the Wicked Do So Well
subheads.17: Does Trouble Really Fall on Them?

verses.text: Then Eliphaz from Teman replied:

“Can anyone do God a favor?
A wise person only helps himself.

Does Shaddai get any pleasure when you do right?
Does he gain anything when your ways are clean?

Is he correcting you because you honor him?
Is that why he brings you to trial?

Is your wickedness not huge?
Do your sins ever stop?

You took clothes as payment for debts from your own brothers, who owed nothing.
You stripped the poor of their clothing.

You gave no water to tired people.
You kept bread from the hungry.

The strong{a} man owned the land,
and the favorite lived on it.

You sent widows away with nothing.
You broke the strength of orphans.

That is why traps surround you
and sudden terror shakes you,

or darkness covers your eyes,
and a flood of water drowns you.

“Is God not high up in heaven?
Look at the tops{b} of the stars, and see how far up they are!

You say, ‘What does God know?
Can he judge us through dark clouds?

The clouds hide him so he cannot see us.
He just walks around on the dome{c} of the sky.’

Will you stay on the old road
that wicked people have walked?

They were swept off before their time.
Their foundations were washed away like a river.

They told God, ‘Go away!’
They asked, ‘What can Shaddai do to them?’{d}

Still, he had loaded their homes with good things.
(The way the wicked plan is not my way.)

Good people see their end and are glad.
The innocent laugh at them and say,

‘Our enemies{e} are truly wiped out,
and fire has burned up whatever they had left.’

“Make peace with God and give in to him.
Then good things will come to you.

Take instruction from his mouth,
and store his words in your heart.

If you come back to Shaddai, you will be rebuilt,
and if you drive evil far from your tent,

if you toss your gold into the dirt,
your fine gold of Ophir{f} among the creek stones,

then Shaddai himself will be your gold,
and your piles of silver.{g}

Then you will find joy in Shaddai
and look up to God.

You will pray, and he will listen,
and you will pay what you promised.

Your plans will work out,
and light will fall across your road.

When people are cast down, you will say, ‘Raise them up!’{h}
and he will rescue the one with downcast eyes.

He will even rescue someone who is guilty.
He will rescue him because your hands are clean.”

notes.text: Original: “the man of arm,” that is, a powerful man.
Original: “head.”
The Hebrew word means the circle or dome of the sky.
This follows the Hebrew. The Septuagint says “What will the Lord do to us?”
The Hebrew word is found only here and is uncertain.
Ophir was a land famous for its fine gold. It may have been in southern Arabia or East Africa. The Septuagint says “Sophir.”
The Hebrew word is rare. It may mean “heaps” or “fine silver.”
Or “pride.” The Hebrew of this verse is uncertain.

subheads.12: Does God See Through the Clouds?

verses.text: Then Job replied:

“Even today my complaint is bitter rebellion.{a}
His{b} hand is heavy on my groaning.

If only I could learn where he is!
If only I could reach his house!

I would present my case in his court
and stock my mouth with arguments.

I would find out the answer he would give,
and grasp what he meant for me.

Would he fight me with all his power?
No, he would listen to me.

An honest man could argue with him there,
and I would be free of my judge for good.

“But I walk east, and he is absent.
I walk west, and I do not see him.

When he works in the north, I catch no glimpse of him.
When he turns south, he stays out of my sight.{c}

But he knows the road I am on.
When he has tested me, I will come out as pure gold.

My feet have stayed in his footprints.
I have followed his path and not wandered away.

I never stepped away from the command of his lips.
I valued what he said above my daily bread.{d}

But he stands alone,{e} and who can change his mind?
Whatever he wants, he does.

He will carry out his plans for me,
and he has many more like them.

So his presence makes me shake.
The more I think, the more I fear him.

God has made my courage melt.
Shaddai has filled me with dread.

Yet the darkness does not keep me quiet,
nor the gloom that covers my face.{f}”

notes.text: The Hebrew word means “rebellion.” The Syriac, the Targum, and the Latin read “bitter.”
This follows the Septuagint and the Syriac. The Hebrew says “my.”
Original: “forward, backward, left, and right,” which may also be read as “east, west, north, and south.”
This follows the Hebrew: “more than my portion.” The Septuagint and the Latin say “in my heart.”
Or “he never changes.” Or, with a small change, “he has chosen.”
The Hebrew of this verse is uncertain.

subheads.1: If Only I Could Find God
subheads.8: He Is Not Here, Yet He Knows Me

verses.text:
“Why does Shaddai set no times for judging?
Why do his friends wait in vain to see his days?{a}

People move boundary stones.
They steal flocks and graze them as their own.

They drive off the orphan’s donkey.
They hold a widow’s ox as a pledge.

They shove the poor off the road.
All the humble of the land have to hide.

Like wild donkeys in the desert,
the poor go out to work, hunting for food.
The wasteland gives bread to their children.

They harvest crops in a field that is not theirs,{b}
and gather leftover grapes in the vineyard of wicked men.

They spend the night naked, with no clothes.
They have no cover against the cold.

They are soaked by mountain rain,
and with no shelter they huddle against rocks.

Evil men snatch the orphan from the breast.
They take the poor man’s coat as a pledge.

The poor go about naked, with no clothing,
and carry sacks of grain while hungry.

Between rows of olive trees{c} they press oil,
and tread winepresses while they are thirsty.

“There is another group: they hate the light.
They do not learn its ways,
and they never walk its paths.

The killer rises when it is light
to murder the poor and needy,
and at night he prowls like a thief.

The adulterer waits for evening to come.
He tells himself, ‘No eye will spot me,’
and he veils his face.

In the dark they dig into houses.
In daytime they lock themselves away.
They want no part of daylight.

For all of them, deep gloom is morning,
because they are friends with the terrors of the dark.

“He{e} is a scrap on the face of the water.
Their land is cursed.
No one turns toward their vineyards.

As drought and heat carry off snow water,
so the grave carries off sinners.

His mother’s womb forgets him. Worms feast on him.
No one remembers him,
and wrong is snapped like a tree.

He preys on{f} the childless woman,
and does no good to the widow.

Yet God{g} drags off the strong with his power.
They get up again, though they had given up hope of living.

He lets them feel safe, and they rest on it,
but his eyes watch their ways.

They are lifted high for a short time and then vanish.
They sink and are collected like all others.
They are cut off like the tips of grain.

If this is not true, who will prove me a liar
and show my words are nothing?”

notes.text: The order of chapters 24–27 is disputed. Some speeches seem to be missing or misplaced: Bildad’s third speech (chapter 25) is very short, Zophar has no third speech, and parts of 24:18–25 and 27:13–23 sound like the friends. Many scholars rearrange these chapters. This book keeps the traditional order.
Original: “his fodder.” Or, dividing the letters differently, “at night.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
The Hebrew word is rare. It may mean the walls of terraces in olive groves.
The Syriac says “God does not listen to their prayer.” The Hebrew says God does not charge folly.
Verses 18–24 are hard. Many think Job is quoting his friends here (“You say...”).
Or “he wrongs.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
Original: “he.”

subheads.1: Why Does God Not Set Times of Judgment?

verses.text: Then Bildad from Shuah replied:

“Rule and awe belong to God.
He keeps peace in the heights of heaven.

Who could count his armies?
On whom does his light not rise?

So how can any mortal be in the right before God?
How could someone born of a woman be clean?

Even the moon is not bright enough for him,
and the stars are not pure in his eyes.

A human is far less, only a maggot.
A person is only a worm!”{a}

notes.text: Bildad’s third speech is very short. Some scholars think part of it is found in 26:5–14. See the note at 24:1.

verses.text: Then Job replied:

“What a help you have been to someone with no strength!
What a rescue for a worn-out arm!

What fine advice you gave to a man with no wisdom,
and what wonderful insight{a} you showed!

Who helped you find those words?
Whose spirit spoke through you?

“The spirits of the dead{b} tremble
under the waters and all who live there.

The grave lies open in front of God,
and Abaddon{c} has no cover.

He stretches the sky of the north over empty space.
He hangs the earth on nothing at all.

He ties up the waters in his rain clouds,
yet the clouds do not burst under the weight.

He hides the round face of the moon{d}
by pulling a cloud across it.

He drew a circle on the face of the water,
where light and darkness meet.

The pillars of heaven shake,
stunned at his roar.

With his power he calmed{e} the sea.
With his skill he crushed Rahab.{f}

His breath cleared the skies,{g}
and his hand pierced the fleeing snake.{h}

These are only the edges of his work.
How small a whisper of him we hear!
Who can grasp the thunder of his great power?”

notes.text: The Hebrew word is the same as in 5:12.
Original: “Rephaim,” the shades of the dead. The Septuagint says “Will giants be born under the water?”
Abaddon means “destruction.” It is a poetic name for the place of the dead (see 28:22; 31:12; Revelation 9:11).
Or “his throne.” The Hebrew words for “throne” and “full moon” are spelled alike.
Or “stirred up.”
Rahab was a sea monster in old stories, a picture of chaos. See the note at 9:13. The Septuagint says “by his wisdom the great sea animal was overthrown.”
The Hebrew word is found only here. It may mean “fair” or “clear.”
Or “the gliding snake,” as in Isaiah 27:1, where it describes Leviathan. The Septuagint says “by his command he killed the rebel dragon.”

verses.text: Job spoke again in a poem{a} and said:

“I swear by God, who is alive and who took away my rights,
and by Shaddai, who has filled my soul with bitterness:

for as long as there is breath in me,
and God’s spirit stays in my nostrils,

my lips will speak nothing false.
My tongue will not whisper a lie.

Never will I say that you are right.
Until my last breath I will hold on to my honesty.

I will keep my goodness and never let it go.
My heart will not blame me for any day of my life.

“May my enemy be treated as the wicked are,
and my attacker as the unjust.

What hope do the godless have when their lives are cut off,
when God takes away their breath?

Will God listen to their cry
when trouble comes down on them?

Will they find joy in Shaddai?
Will they call on God at every hour?

“Let me teach you about God’s hand.
I will not hold back what Shaddai does.

All of you have seen it yourselves.
Why, then, is your talk so empty?

“This is what God hands the wicked man,{b}
the share that cruel people get from Shaddai:

If he has many sons, they are marked for the sword,
and his children will never have enough bread.

Those who outlive him will be buried by disease,{c}
and their widows will not mourn.

He may pile up silver like dirt
and stock clothes like clay.

He can stock them, but good people will wear them,
and innocent people will share the silver.

The house he builds is as frail as a moth’s cocoon,{d}
like a hut a guard puts up.

He goes to bed rich, but he is never gathered to his family.{e}
Then he opens his eyes, and it is all gone.

Terrors flood over him like waters.
A storm wind snatches him in the night.

A scorching wind lifts him up and carries him off.
It sweeps him away from his home.

It hurls itself at him{f} with no pity.
He runs headlong to escape it.

It claps its hands at him
and whistles him out of his place.”

notes.text: The Hebrew word mashal means a saying, a story, or a poem. See also 29:1.
Many scholars think 27:13–23 belongs to the missing third speech of Zophar, since it repeats what the friends teach about the wicked. See the note at 24:1 and compare 20:29.
Original: “by death,” probably a plague. Compare Jeremiah 15:2.
Hebrew “moth.” Some read “spider.” Compare 8:14. The Septuagint says “like moths and like a spider’s web.”
Or, with the Septuagint and the Syriac, “he will do so no more.”
Or “God hurls at him.”

verses.text:
“There is a mine{a} for silver,
and a place where gold is refined.

Iron comes out of the soil,
and rock is melted down into copper.

People push back the darkness.
They search to the farthest limits
for ore in the black depths.

The earth above gives food,
but below it is torn up as if by fire.

Its rocks hold sapphires,{c}
and its dust holds gold.

No hunting bird knows that path.
No falcon{d} has ever seen it.

Stately animals{e} have never stepped on it.
No lion has ever stalked that way.

Workers strike the hard rock.
They flip mountains over from their roots.

They cut tunnels through the stone,
and their eyes spot every treasure.

They block the streams from trickling.
They drag hidden things into the light.

“But where does wisdom come from?
Where is the home of understanding?

No human knows the price of it,{f}
and it cannot be found in the land of the living.

The ocean depths report, ‘It is not here.’
The sea reports, ‘It is not with me.’

Pure gold{g} cannot buy it.
No amount of silver can pay for it.

It is worth more than gold from Ophir,
more than precious onyx{h} or sapphire.

Gold and glass{i} cannot match it.
Fine gold jars cannot trade for it.

Coral and crystal{j} are not worth a mention.
Owning wisdom is worth more than pearls.{k}

Topaz{l} from Cush{m} cannot compare.
Refined gold cannot pay for it.

“Then where does wisdom come from?
Where is the home of understanding?

It is hidden from the eyes of everything alive.
Even the birds of the sky cannot see it.

Abaddon and Death say,
‘We have only heard a rumor of it.’

God understands the way to it.
He alone knows where it lives.

He looks to the ends of the earth
and sees everything under the sky.

When he gave the wind its weight
and measured out the water,

when he made a law for the rain
and charted the route of the lightning,

then he saw wisdom and spoke of it.
He set it up and tested it.

And he told human beings,
‘Respect for the Lord{n} is wisdom,
and turning away from evil is understanding.’”

notes.text: The Hebrew word means “a place of going out,” that is, a mine.
The Hebrew of this verse is hard to read. It seems to describe miners lowered into a shaft on ropes.
The Hebrew word is probably lapis lazuli rather than the sapphire we know today. It appears again in verse 16.
The Hebrew word names a bird of prey. It may be a falcon or a kite.
Original: “sons of pride,” perhaps big wild beasts. The phrase is found only here and in 41:34.
The Septuagint says “its way.”
The Hebrew word is rare. It may mean “closed” (refined) gold.

The Hebrew name of this stone is uncertain. Onyx, carnelian, or lapis lazuli have been suggested. The names of the precious stones in this passage cannot be known for sure. The Septuagint says “gold of Sophir, with precious onyx and sapphire.”
The Hebrew word is found only here. It probably means glass, which was costly then. The Septuagint says “crystal.”
The Hebrew names are both uncertain. They may mean coral and crystal (or jasper). The Septuagint says “coral and fine pearl.”
The Hebrew word may mean pearls, red coral, or rubies. This is uncertain.
The Hebrew word is probably topaz or peridot, which came from an island in the Red Sea. The Septuagint says “the topaz of Ethiopia.”
That is, the upper Nile region.
Hebrew Adonai, “Lord.” It is the only time it is used in Job. Some Hebrew copies are said to read Yahweh.

verses.text: Job spoke again in a poem and said:

“How I wish I could go back to the months of long ago,
to the days when God looked after me,

when his lamp shone over my head,
and his light guided me through the dark,

when I was in the autumn of my life,{a}
and God’s friendship{b} blessed my tent,

when Shaddai was still close by,
and my children{c} gathered around me,

when cream washed my feet,
and rivers of olive oil flowed for me out of the rock!

Whenever I walked to the town gate
and took my chair in the open square,

Young men saw me and stepped aside.
Old men stood up.

Leaders went silent
and pressed their hands to their mouths.

Nobles hushed their voices,
and their tongues stuck to the roofs of their mouths.

Whoever heard me called me happy.
Whoever saw me gave a good report of me.

I saved the poor from their cries for help,
and orphans who had nobody on their side.

A dying man blessed me.
I made a widow’s heart sing for joy.

I wore justice like a coat.
My fairness was my cloak and my turban.

To the blind I was eyes,
and to the lame I was feet.

I was a father to the needy.
I looked into the lawsuits of strangers.

I smashed the teeth of the cruel
and pulled their victims out of their jaws.

“I thought, ‘I will die in my own nest,
and I will have as many days as there are grains of sand.{d}

My roots reach down to water,
and dew rests on my branches all night.

My honor stays fresh with me,
and my bow is strong in my hand.’

“They listened to me and held their breath,
and they waited in silence for my advice.

After I spoke, no one spoke again.
My words fell on them like drops.

They waited for me the way they wait for rain.
They opened their mouths wide for spring showers.

When they had lost hope, I smiled at them,
and they never let my good mood fade.{e}

I picked the path for them and sat at the head.
I lived like a king in the midst of his army,
like one who comforts those in grief.”

notes.text: Original: “the days of my autumn,” that is, the full harvest time of my life.
The Hebrew word means “council” or “close friendship.” Some read “when God protected my tent.”
Or “my young men.”
Or “as the phoenix.” The Hebrew word for “sand” was taken by some ancient Jewish teachers as the name of the long-lived phoenix. The Septuagint says “like the trunk of a palm tree.”
The Hebrew of this verse is uncertain.

subheads.18: Once I Expected a Long Life

verses.text:
“But now I am laughed at
by men younger than I am,
men whose fathers I would not have trusted
to work with my sheepdogs.

What use was their strength to me?
Their energy{a} had long since died.

Hunger and want had made them skin and bone.
They chewed on dry ground,
in the dark{b} of wasteland and ruin.

They picked salty leaves{c} from the shrubs.
They ate roots of the broom bush.{d}

The community drove them out.
People yelled after them as one yells after a thief.

They had to live in dry stream cuts,
in holes in the ground and in the rocks.

They cried out like donkeys among the bushes.
They huddled together under the weeds.{e}

They were foolish people with no name,
thrown out of the land with whips.

“And now I am the subject of their songs.
My name has become a joke to them.

They hate me and stay far away.
They do not even hold back from spitting in my face.

Because God{f} has cut my bowstring and put me down,
they have thrown off all restraint around me.

On my right side a mob{g} rises up.
They knock my feet out from under me
and build ramps of ruin against me.

They pour in as through a wide hole in a wall.
They roll in over the rubble.

Terrors are turned loose on me.
My dignity is blown off like it was chaff,
and my safety has drifted by like a cloud.

“Now my life drains out of me.
Days of suffering have seized me.

At night my bones ache, as if pierced,
and the gnawing pain never rests.

God grabs my clothes with great force,{i}
and chokes me by my collar.

He has flung me into the muck.
I look like dust and ashes.

I cry to you, God, and you give no answer.
I rise to my feet, and you just stare.{j}

You have become hard-hearted toward me.
You strike me with the full force of your hand.

You lift me onto the wind and make me ride it,
then dissolve me in the storm’s roar.{k}

I know you will send me to my death,
to the house set aside for everyone alive.

“Surely no one in a collapsing building refuses to reach out a hand,
or cries for help when disaster comes.{l}

Did I not weep for people in hard times?
Did my heart not ache for the poor?

I hoped for good, and evil came.
I waited for light, and darkness came.

My insides churn and will not settle.
Days of suffering meet me head on.

I wander about in black, though the sun did not burn me.
I get up in the assembly and shout for help.

I have become a brother of jackals
and a friend of ostriches.{m}

My skin turns black and peels off.
My bones burn with fever.

My harp plays only sad songs,
and my flute plays the sound of weeping.”

notes.text: The Hebrew word is the same as in 5:26.
The Hebrew word usually means “yesterday.” Here it may mean “gloom” or “at night.” The Hebrew of this verse is uncertain.
The Hebrew word is found only here. It probably means saltbush, a salty plant the very poor ate. This is uncertain.
The white broom is a desert shrub with bitter roots. Perhaps the roots were burned for warmth instead of eaten.
The Hebrew word is uncertain. It may mean nettles, wild peas, or wild mustard.
Original: “he.” The written Hebrew says “I,” but scribes read “he,” meaning God.
The Hebrew word is found only here. It may mean “brood” or “mob.”
Or “with no one to hold them back.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
This follows the Septuagint. The Hebrew says “my clothing changes shape.” The verse is uncertain.
This follows the Hebrew. One Hebrew copy and the Latin are said to read “you do not look at me.”
The Hebrew has two different readings of the last word. The line is uncertain.
The Hebrew of this verse is uncertain.
Hebrew “daughters of the ostrich.” Some think this means owls. Jackals and ostriches both make sad cries. The Septuagint says “a brother of sea monsters and a friend of ostriches.”

verses.text:
“I made a solemn promise to my eyes.
How could I look at a young woman with desire?

What would God above give me for that?
What would Shaddai on high hand down?

Does disaster not wait for the wicked,
and ruin for those who do evil?

Does God not see how I live
and count every step I take?

“Have I walked with lies?
Has my foot rushed after fraud?

Then weigh me on honest scales,
and let God see that I am blameless.

Have my steps left the right road?
Did my heart chase after what my eyes saw?
Did any dirt stick to my hands?

Then let someone else eat what I plant,
and let my crops{a} be pulled up by the roots.

“Has my heart been tempted by a woman?
Did I lie in wait at my neighbor’s door?

Then let my wife cook for another man,
and let others sleep with her.

That would be a shameful crime,
a sin for judges to punish.

It would be a fire that burns down to Abaddon
and uproots everything I have grown.

“Did I ever brush aside the complaint of a servant, male or female,
when they brought a case against me?

What will I do when God gets up to judge?
What can I say when he questions me?

The God who made me in the womb made them too.
One God shaped both of us before birth.

“Did I refuse the poor what they needed,
or make a widow’s eyes grow dim with tears?

Did I eat my bread alone
while an orphan went without?

(From my youth I raised orphans like a father,
and from birth I guided widows.{b})

Did I see someone dying from lack of clothes,
or a poor man with nothing to wear,

and his body did not thank me,
because I never warmed him with wool from my sheep?

Did I raise my fist against an orphan
because I knew I had friends in the court at the gate?

Then let my shoulder fall from its blade,
and let my arm snap off at the joint.{c}

I was afraid of disaster from God,
and I could not stand against his greatness.

“Did I put my trust in gold,
or call pure gold my security?

Did I celebrate how large my wealth had grown,
or how much my hands had earned?

Did I look at the sun{d} shining,
or the moon moving in its glory,

and feel a secret pull in my heart
and blow a kiss to them with my hand?{e}

That would be another sin for judges to punish,
for I would have denied God above.

“Was I happy when my enemy fell?
Did I cheer when trouble found him?

I never let my mouth sin
by asking for his death in a curse.

Did the people in my tent not say,
‘Who has not had enough of Job’s food?’

No outsider had to spend the night in the street.
My doors stood open to travelers.{f}

Did I hide my sins as people do,{g}
and tuck my guilt away inside me,

because I was afraid of the crowd,
or terrified of the sneers of the clans,
so I kept silent and stayed in the house?

How I wish someone would hear me!
Here is my mark.{h} Let Shaddai reply!
Let my accuser put his charge in writing!

I would carry it on my shoulder with pride.
I would wrap it around my head like a crown.

I would give God an account of every step I took.
Like a prince, I would walk up to him.

“If my land cries out against me,
and all its furrows weep together,

if I ate its harvest without paying,
or broke the spirit of its owners,

then may thorns come up where wheat should be,
and stinking weeds{i} where barley should be.”
Job’s speeches are finished.

notes.text: Or “my children.”
