Original: “her.” The Hebrew of this verse is uncertain; the “her” is probably a widow.
Original: “from its reed,” that is, the upper arm bone.
Original: “the light.”
This was an old way of worshiping the sun or moon.
This follows the ancient versions. The Hebrew says “to the road.”
Or “like Adam.” The Hebrew word is adam, which may mean the first man or just people.
Original: the Hebrew letter taw, the last letter, written as a cross-shaped mark. Here it is Job’s signature on his sworn statement.
The Hebrew word is found only here. It is some harmful weed, perhaps cockle.

subheads.9: If I Have Chased Another Man’s Wife
subheads.13: If I Was Unfair to My Servants

verses.text: These three men gave up answering Job, since in his own eyes he was innocent.

Then a fourth man, Elihu,{a} became angry. He was the son of Barachel{b} from the town of Buz,{c} of the family of Ram. He was angry with Job because Job had made himself out to be more right than God.
He was angry with Job’s three friends as well. They had run out of answers, but they still made Job out to be guilty.{d}
Elihu had held back from talking to Job, since the others were older than he was.
Now he saw that the three men had no reply left, and he burned with anger.

So Elihu, son of Barachel from Buz, spoke up:
“I am young,
and you are very old.
That is why I held back
and was afraid to tell you what I know.

I thought, ‘Let age do the talking.
Let many years teach wisdom.’

Yet a person’s understanding comes from a spirit,
from the breath of Shaddai.

It is not only the old{e} who are wise,
or the aged who know what is fair.

So I say, ‘Hear me out,
and I will share my own knowledge.’

“Look, I held back while you spoke.
I listened closely to your reasons
while you hunted for words.

I gave you my full attention,
and no one among you proved Job wrong.
None of you replied to what he said.

Do not say, ‘We have found wisdom.
Only God can beat him, not a man.’

Job has not aimed his words at me,
and I will not answer him with your arguments.

“They are stunned and have no answer.
They have run out of words.

Should I keep waiting now that they are silent,
now that they stand there and say nothing more?

I will give my share of the answer.
I will tell what I know.

For I am stuffed with words,
and the spirit in me presses hard.

My insides are like wine with no vent,
like new wineskins about to split.

I need to speak so I can feel better.
I need to open my lips and reply.

I will not take sides with anyone,
and I will not flatter anyone.

I have no talent for flattery.
My Maker would take me away at once if I tried.”

notes.text: Elihu means “He is my God.” He is the only speaker in the book with a clearly Israelite name.
Barachel means “God blesses.”
Buz was a son of Nahor, Abraham’s brother (Genesis 22:21). Compare Jeremiah 25:23. The Septuagint adds “of the land of Ausis” (Uz).

This follows the standard Hebrew. An old Jewish tradition says scribes changed the text, and the original read “they had made God look guilty,” because by staying silent they had put God in the wrong.
This follows the Septuagint, the Syriac, and the Latin. The Hebrew says “the great.”

verses.text:
“So now, Job, listen to my speech.
Pay attention to every word I say.

I have opened my mouth now.
My tongue is about to speak.

My words come from a sincere heart.
My lips will say what I truly know.

God’s Spirit formed me,
and Shaddai’s breath keeps me alive.

Reply to me, if you are able.
Arrange your case and take your stand.

In God’s eyes I am the same as you.
I was pinched off{a} from clay too.

You need not be scared of me.
I will not weigh you down.{b}

“You said something I heard clearly.
I caught the sound of your words:

‘I am clean and have not sinned.
I am pure,{c} and there is no guilt in me.

Yet God finds reasons{d} to attack me.
He treats me as his enemy.

He locks my feet in stocks
and watches every path I take.’

Here is my answer: you are wrong in this,
because God is greater than any human.

Why do you complain against him
that he gives no account of what he does?{e}

God speaks once, and then again,
but people do not notice.

He speaks in a dream, in a vision at night,
when deep sleep falls on people,
while they doze on their beds.

Then he opens their ears
and puts his warning on them like a seal,{f}

to turn a person from his actions
and to keep him from pride.

So he holds his soul back from the pit,
and his life from crossing over by the spear.{g}

“Or a person is corrected by pain on his bed,
and by endless aching in his bones.

His appetite turns against bread,
and he hates even his favorite meal.

His flesh wastes away until it can hardly be seen,
and bones that were hidden now stick out.

His soul comes near the pit,
and his life draws near to those who bring death.{h}

But suppose a messenger stands by him,
a spokesman,{i} one in a thousand,
to tell him what is right for him to do.

God shows him kindness and says,
‘Do not let him descend to the pit.
I have found the ransom money for him.’

Then his body becomes fresher{j} than a child’s.
He returns to the days of his youth.

He prays to God and God accepts him.
He sees God’s face with joy,
and God makes him right with himself again.

He bought back my soul from going down to the pit,
and my life will look on the light.’

“God does all these things
two times, even three, for a person,

to bring his soul back from the pit,
so that the light of life can shine on him.

Pay attention, Job, and listen to me.
Be quiet while I talk.

If you have something to say, reply to me.
Go on, for I would like to see you cleared.

Otherwise, listen to me.
Keep silent, and I will pass on wisdom.”

notes.text: That is, pinched off, the way a potter takes a lump of clay.
The Hebrew word is found only here. It may mean “pressure” or “burden.”
The Hebrew word is found only here. It means “clean” or “innocent.”
The Hebrew word is rare. It may mean “pretexts” or “excuses.”
Original: “that he answers none of his words.” Perhaps “that he does not answer for any of his own actions.”
This follows the Hebrew. Or “scares them with warnings.” The Septuagint says “he terrifies them with such frightening visions.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
Or “crossing the river (of death).” The Hebrew word can mean a weapon or a channel.
Or “the angels of death,” or “the place of the dead.”
The Hebrew word means an interpreter or a speaker for someone. Compare 16:20. The Septuagint says “even if a thousand angels of death come, none of them will wound him.”
The Hebrew word is found only here. “Fresher” is a guess from the setting.
Or “it was not worth it to me.”

subheads.19: Pain, a Messenger, and a Ransom
subheads.29: God Brings Back from the Pit

verses.text: Then Elihu went on:

“Listen to my words, you wise men.
Hear me out, you who have knowledge.

The ear tests what it hears,
as the tongue tastes food.

Let us pick out for ourselves what is right.
Let us learn together what is good.

Job has declared, ‘I am innocent,
and God has taken my justice away.

Although I am right, I am called a liar.
My wound{a} cannot be healed, though I did nothing wrong.’

Is there anyone like Job?
He drinks in mockery like water.

He keeps company with evildoers
and walks with wicked men.

For he has said, ‘It does not pay
to take delight in God.’

He rewards people for what they do.
He gives each one the result of his own ways.

It is certain that God will not do wicked things,
and Shaddai will never twist justice.

Who put the earth in his care?
Who set the whole world in its place?{c}

If he turned his attention only to himself,{d}
and took back his spirit and breath,

every living creature would die together,
and humanity would return to dust.

“Use your understanding and listen to this.
Give ear to the sound of what I say.

Could someone who hates justice rule?
Will you condemn the Righteous and Mighty One,

who says to a king, ‘You worthless man!’
and to nobles, ‘You wicked men!’?

He does not favor rulers,
and he does not put the rich ahead of the poor,
for his hands made them all.

They die in an instant, in the dead of night.
People shake and pass away.
The mighty are taken out without a human hand.

His eyes are on every person’s ways,
and he sees each step.

There is no darkness or deep shadow
where evildoers can hide.

God does not need to look into a person again
before he takes him to court.

He breaks the mighty without an investigation
and puts others in their places.

Because he knows what they do,
he overturns them at night, and they are crushed.

He strikes them down as wicked men
where everyone can watch,{e}

because they turned away from following him
and ignored all his ways.

They made the poor cry out to him,
and he heard the cry of the suffering.

When he stays silent, who can blame him?
When he hides his face, who can find him,
whether a nation or one person?

He does this so that godless men will not rule,
and so that no one sets traps for the people.{f}

“Has anyone ever said to God,
‘I have been punished. I will not sin again.

Teach me what I cannot see.
If I have done wrong, I will not do it again’?

Should God pay you back on your terms, since you reject his?
You must decide, not I.
So tell us what you know.

People with understanding will tell me,
and every wise person who hears me will say,

‘Job speaks without knowledge.
His words have no insight.’

I wish Job would be tested all the way,
since he replies like wicked men!

He adds rebellion to his sin.
He claps his hands{g} in scorn among us,
and he piles up words against God.”

notes.text: Original: “my arrow,” that is, the wound made by God’s arrow (compare 6:4).
Original: “men of heart,” that is, men of understanding. The same words are used in verse 34.
The Hebrew does not have “in its place.”
Or “If he set his mind on it.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
Original: “in the place of those who look on.”
The Hebrew of verses 29–33 is very hard to read.
This was a sign of scorn.

subheads.16: God Judges Kings and Poor Alike

verses.text: Then Elihu went on:

“Do you think this is fair?
You say, ‘I am more in the right than God,’

and you ask, ‘What good does it do you?{a}
What do I gain compared to sinning?’

I will give you an answer,
and your friends too.

Look up at the sky and see.
Study the clouds, which are far above you.

If you sin, how does that hurt him?
If your wrongs pile up, what does it do to him?

If you are good, what do you give him?
What does he receive from you?

Your wrong hurts only a person like you.
Your goodness helps only another human.

“People cry out under heavy oppression.
They shout for help against the power of the strong.

But no one asks, ‘Where is God, my Maker,
who gives songs in the night,

who gives us more teaching than the beasts of the field,
and more wisdom than the birds of the sky?’

So they cry out, and he does not answer,
because of the pride of evil people.

God does not listen to empty cries.
Shaddai pays them no attention.

Even less will he hear you when you say you cannot see him,
that your case is before him and you are waiting.

And now you say his anger has never come,
and he takes little notice of foolish pride.{b}

So Job opens his mouth for nothing.
He piles up words without knowledge.”

notes.text: Elihu quotes Job here: “you” means Job himself, or it could be “me.”
The Hebrew word is found only here. It may mean “folly” or “wrongdoing.”

subheads.1: Elihu: God Is Not Harmed by Our Sin

verses.text: Elihu spoke on:

“Stay with me a little longer, and I will show you,
for I have more to say in God’s defense.

I will fetch my knowledge from far away
and give my Maker credit for being just.

My words are not lies.
A man with perfect knowledge stands here with you.

“Look, God is mighty, yet he looks down on no one.
His strength of mind is great.

He will not let the wicked live,
but he gives the poor what is right.

His eyes never leave those who do right.
He sets them on thrones beside kings
and raises them high for good.

If people are tied in chains,
caught in cords of suffering,

he tells them what they have done,
and how proud they have been in their sins.

He uncovers their ears to a lesson
and tells them to quit their evil.

If they obey and serve him,
their days will end in good fortune,
and their years in comfort.

But if they will not listen, they cross over by the spear{a}
and die without knowing why.

“Those whose hearts are godless pile up anger.
Even when he ties them up, they do not cry for help.

They die young,
among the shrine prostitutes.{b}

He rescues the suffering through their suffering
and opens their ears through their pain.

But you are loaded with the verdict meant for the wicked.
Judgment and justice have you in their grip.

Be careful that anger does not tempt you to jeer.
Do not let a large bribe lead you off course.

Will your cries keep you out of trouble,
or all your strong efforts?

Do not wish for the night,
when whole peoples are cut off where they stand.

Watch out! Do not turn to evil,
which you seem to prefer to suffering.

“Look, God is high and powerful.
Who is a teacher like him?

Who has set his road for him?
Who dares tell him, ‘What you did was wrong’?

Remember to praise what he does,
which people have sung about.

All humanity has looked at it.
People see it from a distance.

Yes, God is greater than we can know.
The count of his years cannot be found out.

He pulls up the drops of water.
They fall as rain from his mist,

and the clouds pour it down
and shower it over people in plenty.

Who can understand how the clouds spread out,
or the crashes from his tent?

See how he spreads lightning around himself
and covers the ocean floor.{d}

By these he rules the nations
and gives food in plenty.

He wraps lightning around his hands
and orders it to hit its target.

Its crash tells of him,
and the cattle tell of the storm that rises.{e}”

notes.text: Or “cross the river of death.” See the note at 33:18.
Original: “qedeshim,” men who served as prostitutes at pagan shrines. The point is that their lives end in shame.
The Hebrew of verses 16–20 is very hard to read.
Or “the depths.”
The Hebrew of this verse is very hard to read. The Septuagint says “The Lord will speak about this to his friend, but there is also a share for the unjust.”

subheads.22: God Is Greater Than We Know

verses.text:
“My heart pounds at this,
and jumps from its place.

Hear it! Hear the rumble of his voice,
the growl that rolls from his mouth.

He sends it under the whole sky,
and his lightning to the far ends of the earth.

God’s voice booms in wonderful ways.
His great deeds are past our understanding.

He tells the snow, ‘Fall on the earth,’
and tells the rain shower, ‘Pour down in torrents.’

He puts a seal on everyone’s hands,
so all the people he made will know his work.{b}

Wild animals slip into their hiding places
and wait in their dens.

The storm comes out of its room,
and the cold comes with the winds that scatter.{c}

God’s breath makes ice,
and the wide waters freeze solid.

He fills the thick clouds with water,
and the clouds scatter his lightning.

They swirl around at his direction
to do all that he orders
over the whole inhabited earth.

He makes it come to correct people,
or to water his land,
or to show his faithful love.

“Listen to this, Job.
Stand still and think about the wonders of God.

Do you know how God gives them orders,
and makes the lightning in his clouds flash?

Do you know how the clouds hang in balance,{d}
the marvels of the one with perfect knowledge?

Your clothes grow hot
when the land is hushed under a south wind.

Can you help him stretch out the sky,
hard as a polished metal mirror?

Tell us what to say to him.
We cannot argue our case because of the darkness in our minds.

Should anyone tell him I want to talk?
Who would ask to be wiped out?

People cannot stare at the sun,
shining brightly in the sky,
after the wind has blown the clouds away.

Golden splendor comes from the north.{e}
God is surrounded by awesome glory.

We cannot find Shaddai.
He is great in power,
and he never twists justice or fairness.

So people honor him with awe.
He pays no attention to those who think themselves wise.”{f}

notes.text: Original: “them.”
Or “so that all people may know his work.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
The Hebrew word probably means the north winds. This is uncertain.
The Hebrew word is found only here. It may mean “spreadings” or “balancings.”
Or “golden light.” The Septuagint says “from the north come clouds shining like gold.”
Or “no one who is wise in heart can see him.”

subheads.14: Stop and Think About God’s Wonders

verses.text: Then Yahweh spoke to Job from the middle of a storm:{a}

“Who is this that hides my plans in shadow
with words that show no knowledge?

Get ready like a strong man.{b}
I will ask the questions, and you will answer me.

“Where were you when I built the foundations of the earth?
Speak up, if you are so wise.

Who decided its size? Surely you know!
Who stretched a measuring line across it?

What were its bases set on?
Who laid its cornerstone,

while the morning stars sang as one
and every heavenly being{c} cheered?

“Who closed the sea in with doors
when it burst out as if from the womb,

when I wrapped it in clouds like a robe
and in thick darkness like baby blankets,

when I marked out its limit
and set its bars and doors in place,

when I said, ‘You may come this far, and no farther.
Here your proud waves must stop’?

“In all your life, have you ever ordered the morning to come?
Have you shown the dawn where to stand,

so it can grab the edges of the earth
and shake the wicked out of it?

The earth takes shape like clay pressed by a seal.
Its features stand out like the folds of a coat.{d}

The wicked lose their light,
and the raised arm is broken.

“Have you traveled to the springs that feed the sea?
Have you strolled through the deepest part of the ocean?

Were the gates of death ever opened for you?
Did you ever see the doors of deep darkness?

Have you grasped how far the earth stretches?
Speak, if you know all this.

“Which way leads to where light lives?
And where is the home of darkness,

so you can take each one to its border
and know the paths to its house?

Surely you know, for you were born by then!
You have lived so many years!{e}

“Have you gone into the storerooms of snow?
Have you seen the storerooms of hail,

which I have saved for times of trouble,
for days of fighting and war?

Where does lightning{f} spread out,
or the east wind scatter across the earth?

“Who cut a canal for the flood of rain
and a trail for the thunderbolt,

to bring rain on land where no one lives,
on a desert with no people,

to soak the wild and empty ground
and make the young grass sprout?

Does the rain have a father?
Who is the parent of the dewdrops?

Out of whose body did the ice come?
Who bore the frost that settles from the sky?

Water turns hard as stone,
and the face of the deep freezes over.

“Can you fasten the Pleiades{g} together,
or loosen the straps of Orion?{h}

Can you bring out the Mazzaroth{i} at the right time,
or guide the Bear{j} and its cubs?

Do you know how the sky is ruled?
Can you make it govern the earth?

“Can you call out to the clouds
and be buried in a flood of water?

Can you send out lightning bolts,
and have them answer, ‘Here we are’?

Who gave the ibis{k} its wisdom,
or the rooster its understanding?

Who is clever enough to number the clouds?
Who can pour out the water bottles of the sky,

so the dust turns to mud
and the clods stick together?

“Do you hunt food for the lioness,
or feed the hunger of her cubs,

when they are curled up in their dens
or hiding in the thick brush?

Who provides prey for the raven,
when its chicks cry out to God
and wander about with nothing to eat?”

notes.text: Or “whirlwind.”
Original: “Gird up your loins like a man,” a way of saying “get ready for action.” Or “like a warrior.”
Original: “sons of God.” See the note at 1:6. The Septuagint says “all my angels praised me with a loud voice.”
This pictures dawn bringing out the shapes of the land, as a seal makes marks on clay. The Septuagint is very different: “Did you take clay from the ground and form a living creature?”
Yahweh is being playful: Job could not have been alive at creation.
Or “light.”
The Hebrew name is Kimah, a star cluster usually taken to be the Pleiades. Compare 9:9.
The Hebrew name Kesil means “fool.” It is usually taken as Orion, pictured as a giant tied in the sky. These star names are traditional, not certain.
The Hebrew word is found only here. It may mean the star groups of the zodiac, or one star group. The Septuagint keeps “Mazuroth” and adds “the evening star with its rays.”
The Hebrew name Ayish is probably the Great Bear and its “children,” the stars of its tail. Others suggest Aldebaran or the Hyades. Compare 9:9.

The Hebrew words for “ibis” and “rooster” are rare and uncertain. The ibis (linked to the Egyptian god of wisdom) and the rooster (which announces dawn) were both thought to sense the weather. The Septuagint says “Who gave women skill in weaving or the knowledge of fine needlework?”

subheads.16: Have You Seen the Deep and the Dark?

verses.text:
“Do you know when mountain goats{a} give birth?
Have you watched deer{b} bring forth their young?

Can you figure out how long they are pregnant?
Do you know when they are due,

when they crouch down, deliver their young,
and their labor pains are over?

Their young grow stout in open fields.
They go off and do not return.

“Who set the wild donkey{c} free?
Who untied the ropes of the swift donkey?

I gave it the wasteland as its home,
and the salt flats as its place to live.

It scoffs at the clamor of towns.
It never hears a driver yell.

It roams the hills for its pasture
and searches out anything green.

“Would the wild ox{d} agree to work for you?
Would it spend the night at your feed bin?

Can you tie it to a plow with a rope?
Will it pull your harrow through the valley?

Will you depend on it because it is so strong,
and leave your hard work to it?

Will you trust it to haul your grain home
and pile it on your threshing floor?

“The ostrich{e} flaps her wings happily,
but do her wings and feathers compare with the stork’s?{f}

In the dirt she leaves her eggs,
and the warm sand hatches them.

She forgets that a foot could crush them,
or that wild beasts could stamp on them.

She is rough with her chicks, as though they belonged to another.
She does not worry that her work may be wasted,

because God took away her wisdom
and gave her no good sense.

Yet when she leaps up to race,{g}
she mocks horse and rider.

“Did you give the horse its power?
Did you cover its neck with a shaking mane?{h}

Do you teach it to hop like a locust?
Its proud snort is frightening.

It scrapes{i} the valley floor, glad of its strength,
and gallops out against the weapons.

It mocks fear and never flinches.
It does not shy from the sword.

The arrows rattle on its side,
with the flash of the spear and the lance.

Trembling with excitement, it swallows up the ground.
When the trumpet sounds, it cannot stand still.

At each blast of the trumpet it snorts, ‘Ha!’
It smells battle from far away,
the shouts of commanders and the war cries.

“Is the hawk{j} wise because of you,
when it stretches its wings toward the south?

Do you order the eagle{k} to rise
and build its nest up high?

It lives on the cliff and spends the night there,
on a rocky point and a mountain fort.

From there it hunts for food.
Its eyes see far into the distance.

Its chicks feed on blood,
and where there are dead bodies, there it is.”

notes.text: The Hebrew means “climbers of the rock,” probably the Nubian ibex.
The Hebrew word means female deer.
Two Hebrew words (pere and arod) both mean the wild donkey or onager, a fast desert animal that cannot be tamed. The second word is found only here.
Hebrew re’em, the aurochs, a powerful wild ox with horns that is now extinct. The Septuagint says “one-horned,” which older English Bibles turned into “unicorn.”

The Hebrew word, found only here, means “shrieking ones.” It is usually taken to be the ostrich, which fits what follows. The Septuagint says “The peacock has a lovely wing; if the stork and ostrich conceive...” This is likely but not certain.
Or “are they the wings of the kind one?” The Hebrew word for stork sounds like the word for “faithful love.” The Hebrew of this line is uncertain.
The meaning of the Hebrew verb is uncertain.
The Hebrew word is found only here. It may mean “thunder,” “trembling,” or “mane.” The Septuagint says “terror.”
Original: “They paw.”
The Hebrew word names a falcon or hawk. The idea may be the hawk flying south for winter.
The Hebrew word can mean an eagle or a griffon vulture. Verse 30 fits the vulture.

verses.text: Yahweh went on and said to Job:

“Will the one who finds fault argue with Shaddai?
Let the man who corrects God answer for it.”
Then Job replied to Yahweh:

“I am nothing. How can I answer you?
I will clap my hand over my mouth.

I spoke once and have no reply.
I spoke again, and I will say no more.”
Yahweh then addressed Job once more, speaking out of the storm:

“Get ready like a strong man.{a}
I will ask the questions, and you will answer me.

Would you really cancel my justice?
Would you call me guilty so that you can be innocent?

Is your arm as strong as God’s?
Can you thunder with a voice like his?

“Go ahead, dress yourself in glory and greatness.
Put on splendor and honor.

Pour out your angry floods.
Look at each proud person and bring him down.

Look at all the proud and make them small.
Stamp out the wicked wherever they stand.

Bury every one of them in the dust.
Lock them away in the dark place of the dead.

Then I myself will praise you,
because your own right hand has won the victory for you.

“Look at Behemoth,{b} made by me just as you were.
He eats grass like a bull.

See the power in his hips
and the strength in his belly muscles.

His tail sways stiff as a cedar.
The sinews of his thighs{c} are knotted tight.

His bones are pipes of bronze.
His legs are rods of iron.

“Among God’s works he stands first.{d}
No one but his Maker dares bring a sword near him.

The hills grow his food,
and all the wild animals frolic nearby.

Beneath lotus plants{e} he lies down,
in the shelter of reeds and marsh.

Lotus plants shade him with their branches.
Willows along the stream surround him.

A raging river does not scare him.
He stays calm even when the Jordan{f} rushes up to his mouth.

Can anyone catch him while he watches,
or pierce his nose with a snare?”

notes.text: Original: “Gird up your loins like a man,” a way of saying “get ready for action.” See the note at 38:3.

Hebrew behemot, a plural form of the word for “beast,” used here to mean “the Great Beast.” It fits the hippopotamus best, though some think of the elephant or a creature of legend. The Septuagint says “Look now at the wild animals with you.” This is uncertain.
The Hebrew word is found with this meaning only here. Some take it differently.
Or “the chief of God’s works.” The Septuagint says “the chief of the Lord’s creation, made to be played with by his angels.”
The Hebrew word is found only here and in verse 22. It probably means the thorny lotus bush. The Septuagint says “trees of every kind, by the papyrus, and reed, and bulrush.”
That is, any great river in flood.

verses.text:
“Can you pull Leviathan{a} out with a fishhook,{b}
or tie down his tongue with a rope?

Can you thread a cord through his nose,
or pierce his jaw with a hook?

Will he plead with you over and over for mercy?
Will he speak softly to you?

Will he sign a treaty with you
to serve as your slave for life?

Will you play with him like a pet bird,
or put him on a leash for your daughters?

Will fishing crews bargain over him?
Will they cut him up and sell him among the merchants?

Can you riddle his skin with harpoons,
or his head with fishing spears?

Put your hand on him once,
and you will never forget the fight, and never try again!

“Anyone who hopes to beat him is let down.{c}
Is a man not knocked flat just by seeing him?

No one is bold enough to stir him up.
So who can stand against me?

Who has given me anything first, so that I owe him?{d}
Everything under all the sky is mine.

“I must speak of his limbs,
his great power, and his fine shape.

Who can peel off his outer coat?
Who can get inside his double armor?{e}

Who can pry open the doors of his mouth?
His teeth are ringed with terror.

His back is made of rows of shields,{f}
sealed up tight together.

Each is so close to the next
that not even air can slip between.

Each one clings to the next.
They are locked together and cannot be pried apart.

His sneezes throw off flashes of light.
His eyes shine like the first rays of dawn.{g}

Flames shoot from his mouth.
Sparks of fire fly out.

Smoke pours from his nose,
like steam from a boiling pot over a reed fire.

His breath lights coals on fire,
and a blaze comes out of his mouth.

Strength lives in his neck,
and terror dances in front of him.

The folds of his flesh are welded together,
solid and unmoving.

His heart is solid as stone,
solid as the lower millstone.

When he rises up, even the mighty{h} are afraid.
When he thrashes, they lose their senses.

A sword that hits him does no good,
nor does a spear, an arrow, or a dart.{i}

To him iron is like straw,
and bronze is like rotten wood.

Arrows do not make him run.
Slingstones are like husks to him.

Clubs are like stubble to him.
He laughs at the whistle of a flying spear.

His belly has sharp shards like broken pots.
He drags across the mud like a threshing sled.

He churns the deep until it bubbles like a pot.
He stirs the sea like a pot of perfume.

He leaves a shining wake behind him.
You would think the ocean had gray hair.

Nothing on earth is like him,
a creature made to have no fear.

He looks down on everything proud.
He is king over all the beasts of pride.”{j}

notes.text: Hebrew Livyatan. See the note at 3:8. This is often thought to describe the crocodile, but it is made larger with features of a sea monster, such as fire from the mouth (verses 18–21). Its identity is uncertain. In the Hebrew text, 41:1–8 is numbered 40:25–32, and 41:9–34 is 41:1–26.
Or “a hook.”
Original: “his hope is false,” that is, the hope of anyone who would attack him.
The Hebrew of verses 10–11 is hard. Some copies and the Septuagint say “Who can stand before him? Who has faced him and come out safe?” Compare Romans 11:35.
This follows the Septuagint, “inside the fold of his breastplate.” The Hebrew says “his double bridle,” perhaps meaning the jaws.
Or “His pride is his rows of shields.” The Hebrew words for “pride” and “back” differ only in their vowels.
The Septuagint says “When he sneezes a light shines, and his eyes look like the morning star.”
Or “the gods.”
The Hebrew word is found only here. It may mean “javelin” or “coat of armor.”
Original: “sons of pride,” also in 28:8. They are probably proud wild animals. The Septuagint says “he is king of everything in the waters.”

verses.text: Job answered Yahweh:

“You can do anything, I know.
Nothing you plan can be blocked.

You asked, ‘Who is this that hides my plans without knowing what he says?’
I spoke about things I did not understand,
things too wonderful for me to know.

You said, ‘Now listen, and I will speak.
I will question you, and you will tell me the answers.’

I used to know you only by what others said.
Now my own eyes have seen you.

So I take back what I said,{a}
and I am sorry{b} in dust and ashes.”
When Yahweh had said all this to Job, he turned to Eliphaz from Teman. He said, “My anger is aimed at you and your two friends. You have not told the truth about me the way my servant Job has.

So choose seven bulls and seven rams. Take them to Job, my servant, and burn them as an offering for yourselves. He will pray on your behalf, and I will grant his request. Then I will not treat you as your foolishness deserves. You were wrong about me, but Job spoke truly.”
So Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar, who came from Teman, Shuah, and Naamah, went and did as Yahweh had told them. And Yahweh accepted Job’s prayer.
Job prayed for his friends, and then Yahweh gave back everything he had lost.{c} In fact, Yahweh doubled all that Job had owned.

All of Job’s brothers and sisters came, and so did everyone who had known him before. In his house they shared a meal with him. They felt sorry for him and cheered him up after all the trouble Yahweh had sent. Every guest handed him a piece of silver{d} and a gold ring.{e}
The last years of Job’s life were even more blessed by Yahweh than the first. His herds and flocks grew to 14,000 sheep and 6,000 camels. He also owned 1,000 pairs of oxen and 1,000 female donkeys.
Seven sons{f} and three daughters were also born to him.
The oldest daughter he called Jemimah.{g} The next was Keziah,{h} and the youngest was Keren-happuch.{i}
Job’s daughters were the loveliest women anywhere in the country. Their father also let them inherit land, just as their brothers did.
After this, Job lived another 140 years.{j} He saw his children and grandchildren, four generations in all.
Then Job died, an old man who had lived a full life.{k}

notes.text: Or “I despise my words,” or “I melt away.” The Hebrew verb has no stated object. The Septuagint says “So I have counted myself worthless, and I faint.” This verse is very hard to translate.
Or “I am comforted,” or “I change my mind about dust and ashes,” that is, about being mortal or about my grief. The Hebrew word can mean several things.
Or “restored his fortunes.” Original: “turned the captivity of Job.”

Original: “a qesitah,” a piece of money or weight of unknown value. It is found elsewhere only in Genesis 33:19 and Joshua 24:32. The Septuagint says “a lamb.” The Aramaic Targum of Job from Qumran is said to end at this verse.
Or “a nose ring” or “an earring.” The Septuagint says “four drachmas’ weight of gold.”
The Hebrew form for “seven” is unusual. Some Jewish teachers took it to mean “twice seven,” that is, fourteen sons.
Jemimah probably means “dove.” The Septuagint has “Day.”
Keziah means “cassia,” a sweet-smelling spice.
Keren-happuch means “horn of eye paint,” a small container for the makeup used to darken eyelids. The Septuagint has “Amaltheia’s horn,” the horn of plenty.
The Septuagint says Job lived 170 years after his suffering, 240 years in all.

The Septuagint adds a long closing note. It says Job will rise again with those the Lord raises up, that he lived in the land of Ausis on the border of Edom and Arabia, that he was first called Jobab, and that he married an Arabian woman and had a son named Ennon. It then gives his family line, going back to Esau and to Abraham.
